This short notebook teaches you how the course notebooks work before you start a module: running
code chunks, changing a line of code, reading an error message, typing your answers and knitting
the report. It takes about 20 minutes. Do it after the setup steps (Steps 1 to 4) in the
[Getting Started guide](../docs/getting-started.md).

You will use one small dataset: the number of people who died from injuries at work in the US each
year, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI).

Before you start, **save a copy under your own name**: File > Save As..., in this same `practice`
folder, for example `first_steps_lastname.Rmd`.

# Step 1. Run your first chunk

The grey box below is a **code chunk**. Click the green triangle at its top right (or put your
cursor inside it and press Ctrl + Shift + Enter; Cmd + Shift + Enter on a Mac).

```{r first-chunk}
2 + 2
```

The answer, `[1] 4`, appears below the chunk (or in the Console). The `[1]` just means "first
value".

Now run this one. Text after `#` is a **comment**: R ignores it, so it is a place for notes.

```{r dates}
Sys.Date()   # today's date
```

# Step 2. Save a result with a name

`<-` saves a value under a name (an **object**) so you can use it later. Run the chunk, then look
at the **Environment** pane (top right): `deaths_2022` and `deaths_2021` are listed there.

```{r objects}
deaths_2022 <- 5486
deaths_2021 <- 5190
deaths_2022 - deaths_2021
```

Nothing prints when you save an object; typing its name (or doing a calculation with it) prints
the value.

# Step 3. Load packages and data

Every course notebook starts with a chunk like this one, called **setup**. It loads the
**packages** (extra functions installed by `install_packages.R`) and reads the data. **Always run
the setup chunk first**, and run it again whenever you reopen RStudio.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)    # reading CSV files
library(dplyr)    # filtering and summarising tables
library(ggplot2)  # charts

# Read the data from the CFOI module's folder, or from GitHub if the file is not there
local <- "../modules/us-bls-cfoi/data/tidy/cfoi_national.csv"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/us-bls-cfoi/data/tidy/cfoi_national.csv")
fatal <- read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else github, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

`fatal` is now in the Environment pane. Click the small table icon at the right of its row (or
type `View(fatal)` in the Console) to see the whole table in a new tab, like a spreadsheet.

# Step 4. Look at the data

```{r look}
nrow(fatal)   # number of rows
names(fatal)  # column names
head(fatal)   # the first six rows
```

Each row is one count: the number of `fatalities` in one `year`, for one `category` of one
`group` (for example the group `Gender`, category `Women`). The row with group `All` is the total.

# Step 5. Pick rows with `filter()`

`filter()` keeps the rows that match a condition. `|>` means "and then": it passes the table on
to the next line.

```{r total}
fatal |>
  filter(group == "All") |>
  select(year, fatalities)
```

Two equals signs (`==`) test whether two things are equal; one (`=`) is used for something else.
Text goes in quotes: `"All"`.

**Try it:** in the chunk below, change `2022` to another year between 2011 and 2021 and run it
again.

```{r one-year}
fatal |>
  filter(group == "Gender", year == 2022) |>
  select(year, category, fatalities)
```

# Step 6. Make a chart

`ggplot()` draws charts. `aes()` says which columns go on which axis; each `+` adds a layer.

```{r chart}
fatal |>
  filter(group == "All") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = fatalities)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +   # start the y axis at zero
  labs(title = "Fatal work injuries in the US", x = NULL, y = "Deaths")
```

**Try it:** change `geom_line()` to `geom_col()` (and delete the `geom_point()` line and its `+`)
to make a bar chart.

# Step 7. Read an error message

Errors are normal; reading them is a skill. This chunk has a typo. Run it and read the red message.

```{r error-practice, error = TRUE}
fatal |>
  filter(group == "Gender", year == 2022) |>
  select(year, catgory, fatalities)
```

The message says that the column `catgory` doesn't exist. **Fix the typo** (it should be
`category`) and run the chunk again.

Other messages you are likely to see:

- `could not find function "filter"`: the packages are not loaded. Run the setup chunk.
- `object 'fatal' not found`: the data are not loaded (run the setup chunk), or the name is
  misspelled. R is case-sensitive: `Fatal` is not `fatal`.
- A `+` in the Console instead of `>`: R is waiting for you to finish a line, often because of a
  missing `)`. Click in the Console and press Esc.

# Step 8. Your turn

Run the chunk, then answer the questions below it.

```{r events}
fatal |>
  filter(group == "Event or exposure", year == 2022,
         category_code %in% c("E1X", "E2X", "E3X", "E4X", "E5X", "E6X")) |>
  arrange(desc(fatalities)) |>
  select(category, fatalities)
```

These are the main kinds of event that caused the deaths.

**Questions**

1. How many people died from injuries at work in the US in 2022? In which year from 2011 to 2022
   were there the fewest deaths? (Use the tables in Step 5.)
2. Roughly what share of the people who died at work in 2022 were women? Why might the share be
   so small?
3. Which kind of event caused the most deaths in 2022? Did that surprise you?

**Your answer:**

Type your answers here, outside the grey chunks. Leave a blank line between paragraphs. A line
that starts with `- ` becomes a bullet point, and `**two stars**` make text **bold**.



# Step 9. Knit the report

1. Save the notebook (Ctrl + S, or Cmd + S on a Mac).
2. Click **Knit** (the ball of yarn at the top of this pane). If RStudio offers to install or
   update packages, click Yes.
3. A preview of the report opens, and an HTML file with the same name as your notebook is saved
   in the `practice` folder. That HTML file is what you submit for the course notebooks.

Knitting runs every chunk again from the top in a fresh session, so it only works if the chunks
run in order. If knitting fails, the message names the chunk with the problem.

**Checklist** before you start a module:

- [ ] I can run a chunk and see its output.
- [ ] I ran the setup chunk first.
- [ ] I changed a line of code and ran it again.
- [ ] I fixed an error.
- [ ] I typed an answer and knitted the report to HTML.

You are ready. Open a module's `README.md`, then its starter notebook for your course.
